questions.question: What is Amazon CloudFront and what problem does it solve?
questions.answer: CloudFront is AWS's Content Delivery Network (CDN) service. It solves two main problems: high latency for global users (by caching content at 400+ edge locations near users worldwide) and security concerns (by allowing S3 buckets to remain private via OAC while still serving content globally).

questions.question: What is an edge location in CloudFront?
questions.answer: An edge location is a mini data center in a city (separate from AWS regions and AZs) where CloudFront caches copies of your content. There are 400+ edge locations worldwide. When a user requests content, CloudFront serves it from the nearest edge location instead of from the origin — this dramatically reduces latency.

questions.question: What is OAC and why is it important?
questions.answer: OAC stands for Origin Access Control. It is a CloudFront security mechanism that grants only a specific CloudFront distribution permission to access a private S3 bucket. The S3 bucket policy is updated to allow s3:GetObject only from the CloudFront service principal with a condition matching the distribution ARN. This means the bucket never needs to be made public — only CloudFront can read from it.

questions.question: What three things must you provide when creating a CloudFront distribution for an S3 static website?
questions.answer: 1) Origin — the S3 bucket URL (source of content). 2) Default Root Object — the filename to serve for the root URL, typically index.html. 3) Origin Access Control (OAC) — the permission mechanism that allows CloudFront to access the private S3 bucket on behalf of users.

questions.question: What is Route 53 and what does 'authoritative name server' mean?
questions.answer: Route 53 is AWS's DNS (Domain Name System) service. An authoritative name server has the final, definitive answer for the DNS records in its hosted zone. When another DNS resolver asks 'what is the IP for myshop.com?', Route 53 gives the authoritative answer — it doesn't forward the question elsewhere, it is the source of truth for that domain.

questions.question: What is a hosted zone in Route 53?
questions.answer: A hosted zone is a container in Route 53 that stores all DNS records for a specific domain (e.g., myshop.com). When you create a hosted zone, Route 53 assigns 4 name servers. You configure your domain registrar to use these name servers, making Route 53 authoritative for your domain. Inside the hosted zone, you create records like A, CNAME, MX, etc.

questions.question: What is Boto3 and how is it different from the AWS CLI?
questions.answer: Boto3 is the official AWS SDK for Python. It is a Python library that lets developers interact with AWS services (EC2, S3, DynamoDB, etc.) from within Python code. The AWS CLI is a command-line tool for terminal commands. Boto3 is used to embed AWS calls inside application business logic; CLI is for terminal scripts, quick commands, and pipelines. Both use the same underlying AWS APIs and share the same credentials configured via aws configure.

questions.question: What does aws configure do and what information does it ask for?
questions.answer: aws configure sets up AWS credentials locally on your machine. It prompts for: (1) AWS Access Key ID, (2) AWS Secret Access Key, (3) Default region name (e.g., ap-south-1), and (4) Default output format (e.g., json). These credentials are stored locally and used by both the AWS CLI and Boto3 SDK to authenticate with AWS.

questions.question: What is the difference between a cache hit and a cache miss in CloudFront?
questions.answer: A cache hit occurs when a user requests content and CloudFront already has it cached at the nearest edge location — it is served immediately with very low latency. A cache miss occurs when the edge location does not have the content — CloudFront must fetch it from the origin (S3), cache it, then serve it. Cache misses are slower but future requests for the same content become cache hits.

questions.question: Why are AMI IDs region-specific in AWS?
questions.answer: AWS maintains separate registries of AMI images in each region. The same operating system (e.g., Ubuntu Server 22.04 LTS) has a different AMI ID in each region because each region stores its own copy of that image, with its own unique identifier. When writing a Boto3 script that launches EC2 in ap-south-1, you must use the AMI ID from the ap-south-1 registry — not from us-east-1.

questions.question: Scenario: You deploy a new website version to S3 but CloudFront is still showing the old version to users. How do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) CloudFront edge caches still hold the old version — TTL hasn't expired yet. (Task) Force edge caches to evict the stale content immediately. (Action) Create a CloudFront cache invalidation for the path /* (to invalidate all files). This tells all edge locations worldwide to delete their cached copy. (Result) The next user request to each edge location triggers a cache miss, fetching the updated content from S3. Note: First 1,000 invalidation paths per month are free.

questions.question: Scenario: Your S3 bucket is public and your company's security team is demanding it be made private immediately, but the website must stay accessible. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) Public S3 bucket is a security risk. (Task) Remove public access while maintaining website availability. (Action) 1) Create a CloudFront distribution with OAC for the S3 bucket. 2) Update the S3 bucket policy to allow s3:GetObject only from the CloudFront distribution ARN. 3) Enable 'Block all public access' on the S3 bucket. 4) Remove the old public bucket policy. 5) Update users/DNS to use the CloudFront endpoint instead of the S3 URL. (Result) Bucket is private; website is accessible via CloudFront with global low latency.

questions.question: Scenario: A customer wants to access your website via www.myshop.com instead of the CloudFront URL. What AWS services and steps are needed?
questions.answer: (Situation) Users need a friendly domain name. (Task) Map www.myshop.com to CloudFront. (Action) 1) Register/transfer myshop.com to Route 53 or update registrar NS to Route 53 name servers. 2) Create a hosted zone for myshop.com in Route 53. 3) Add an SSL certificate for myshop.com in ACM in us-east-1. 4) Add www.myshop.com as an Alternate Domain Name (CNAME) in the CloudFront distribution. 5) Attach the ACM certificate to the distribution. 6) Create an A record (Alias) in Route 53 pointing www.myshop.com to the CloudFront distribution. (Result) Users type www.myshop.com → Route 53 resolves to CloudFront → content served over HTTPS.

questions.question: Scenario: A Boto3 EC2 launch script runs, prints an instance ID, but instance.public_ip_address returns None. What is wrong and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: (Situation) Instance was created but public IP is None. (Task) Retrieve the assigned public IP after the instance is running. (Action) Call instance.reload() after instance.wait_until_running(). The Python instance object was created at launch time with incomplete data (IP was not yet assigned). reload() fetches the current state from AWS including the now-assigned public IP and private IP. (Result) instance.public_ip_address returns the correct IP.

questions.question: Scenario: Your company runs a web app in ap-south-1. Users in Australia complain about slow load times. You have a budget to expand to only one additional region. What Route 53 routing policy would help most?
questions.answer: (Situation) High latency for Australian users, single region. (Task) Route Australian users to a geographically closer resource. (Action) Deploy the app in ap-southeast-2 (Sydney). Use Route 53 Latency-Based Routing — create records for both ap-south-1 and ap-southeast-2. Route 53 will automatically route each user to the region with lowest latency for them. (Result) Australian users go to Sydney endpoint; Indian users stay on Mumbai endpoint. No need to manage geography manually.

questions.question: Scenario: You need to test a new version of your application. You want only 10% of traffic to go to the new version while 90% goes to the stable version. What do you do?
questions.answer: (Situation) A/B testing — two versions, controlled traffic split. (Task) Route 90% to v1 and 10% to v2. (Action) Use Route 53 Weighted Routing. Create two A records for the same domain — assign weight 90 to v1 endpoint and weight 10 to v2 endpoint. Route 53 distributes traffic proportionally based on the weights. (Result) 10% of users test the new version; 90% stay on stable. If v2 succeeds, adjust weights gradually to 50/50, then 100 to v2.

questions.question: Scenario: A Python developer's Boto3 script fails with 'AuthFailure: Not authorized' when trying to launch EC2. What are the possible causes?
questions.answer: (Situation) Boto3 script fails authentication. (Task) Diagnose and fix auth error. (Action) Check: 1) Were credentials configured via aws configure with a valid Access Key and Secret? 2) Does the IAM user or role have ec2:RunInstances permission? 3) Does the IAM policy also include ec2:CreateTags if TagSpecifications is used? 4) Is the region in the script matching the region the credentials are valid for? 5) Have the access keys been deactivated or deleted in IAM? (Result) Fix the missing permission or expired/invalid credential, then re-run.

questions.question: Scenario: After migrating a domain's NS records from GoDaddy to Route 53, some users see the new site and others see the old one. Why?
questions.answer: (Situation) Mixed routing behavior after NS migration. (Task) Understand and manage the transition. (Action) This is DNS propagation delay. Different recursive DNS resolvers worldwide cached the old NS records and will serve them until their individual TTLs expire. As each resolver's cache expires, it fetches the new Route 53 NS records and starts routing correctly. (Result) Full propagation takes up to 48 hours (usually faster). Users will gradually all reach the new site — no action needed.

questions.question: Scenario: A developer uploaded 10,000 files to S3 and needs them immediately visible via CloudFront without waiting for TTL to expire. Is cache invalidation feasible?
questions.answer: (Situation) Large update, need immediate propagation. (Task) Invalidate cache efficiently. (Action) Use a single invalidation path /* which matches all files. This counts as one invalidation path — not 10,000. This is far more efficient. Note: The first 1,000 invalidation paths/month are free; additional paths cost $0.005 each. (Result) All edge caches evict their content; next requests fetch fresh files from S3. Consider versioning file names (e.g., main.v2.js) as an alternative to invalidation for very high-frequency updates.

questions.question: Scenario: A Boto3 script needs to upload a resume PDF from a Python web app to a specific S3 path based on the applicant's name. Write the logic.
questions.answer: (Situation) Web app needs to store user uploads in S3. (Task) Upload a file to a structured S3 path. (Action) Use boto3.client('s3').upload_file(). Construct the S3 key as f'resumes/{applicant_name}/resume.pdf'. Call s3.upload_file(local_file_path, bucket_name, s3_key). Wrap in try/except to handle upload failures gracefully. (Result) Files are organized in S3 by applicant name (e.g., resumes/Rohan_Sharma/resume.pdf) — easy to query and manage.

questions.question: Compare OAC and OAI in CloudFront. Which should you use and why?
questions.answer: OAI (Origin Access Identity) is the older mechanism for giving CloudFront access to a private S3 bucket. It uses a special CloudFront user identity added to the bucket policy. OAC (Origin Access Control) is the modern replacement. OAC supports features OAI doesn't: server-side encryption with AWS KMS (SSE-KMS), S3 Object Lambda, and multi-region access points. AWS has deprecated OAI and recommends OAC for all new distributions. If you have existing OAI-based distributions, AWS recommends migrating to OAC.

questions.question: Explain the full end-to-end request flow when a user visits www.myshop.com, which is served by S3 + CloudFront + Route 53.
questions.answer: 1) User types www.myshop.com in browser. 2) Browser queries its local DNS resolver. 3) Resolver queries Route 53 (authoritative). 4) Route 53 returns the CloudFront distribution endpoint (d111abc.cloudfront.net) via A Alias record. 5) Browser connects to the nearest CloudFront edge location. 6) Edge checks cache — cache hit? Serve immediately. Cache miss? Edge requests content from origin (private S3 bucket) using OAC credentials. 7) S3 verifies the bucket policy allows this CloudFront distribution, returns content. 8) Edge caches content (for TTL duration) and serves to user. 9) All future users from the same region get a cache hit.

questions.question: Why must SSL/TLS certificates for CloudFront be in us-east-1? What happens if you create them in a different region?
questions.answer: CloudFront is a global service with no single home region — it is managed from a control plane in us-east-1. When you attach an ACM certificate to a distribution, CloudFront reads certificates from ACM in us-east-1. If you create a certificate in ap-south-1 or any other region, it simply will not appear in the CloudFront console as an option — you cannot select it. The certificate must exist in us-east-1 even if your origin is in Mumbai. This is a common exam trap.

questions.question: Design an architecture for a high-availability global static website with a custom domain, private S3, global low latency, HTTPS, and automatic failover.
questions.answer: Architecture: 1) S3 bucket in ap-south-1 with Block Public Access enabled. Upload static assets. 2) CloudFront distribution with S3 as origin, OAC enabled, HTTPS enforced, and price class All Regions. 3) ACM SSL certificate for custom domain in us-east-1, attached to CloudFront. 4) Route 53 hosted zone for custom domain. A Alias record pointing to CloudFront. 5) For failover: use Route 53 health checks on the CloudFront endpoint, with a secondary failover record pointing to a backup site or error page. 6) Enable CloudFront access logging to S3 for monitoring. 7) Optionally add AWS WAF to CloudFront for security filtering. Result: Globally available, private, HTTPS-secured, custom-domain website with automatic failover.

questions.question: How does Boto3 authenticate with AWS and what are the credential resolution options?
questions.answer: Boto3 uses a credential chain — it looks for credentials in this order: (1) Explicitly passed credentials in the boto3.client() call (not recommended for production). (2) Environment variables: AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY. (3) AWS credentials file (~/.aws/credentials) configured via aws configure. (4) AWS config file (~/.aws/config). (5) IAM instance profile (if running on EC2) — the EC2 instance's attached IAM role provides temporary credentials automatically via the instance metadata service. In production, IAM roles (option 5) are preferred — no credentials stored on disk, automatically rotated by AWS.
